BOURBAKI SEMINAR
32nd year, 1979/80, no. 543
November 1979

THE FUNDAMENTAL GROUP OF THE COMPLEMENT
OF A PLANE CURVE HAVING ONLY ORDINARY
DOUBLE POINTS IS ABELIAN

[after W. FULTON]

by Pierre DELIGNE

Introduction

THEOREM 1.- Let C ⊂ ℙ²(ℂ) be a plane curve whose only singularities are double points with distinct tangents. Then the fundamental group of ℙ²(ℂ) - C is abelian.

This theorem was stated by Zariski in 1929 ([8]). See also [9], Ch. VIII. His proof used Severi's theorem, according to which the space of irreducible plane curves of a given degree having a given number of double points is irreducible (Vorlesungen über algebraische Geometrie, 1921, Anhang F). It is still unknown whether Severi's assertion is true or false.

The π₁ considered in the theorem is the genuine fundamental group, the topologists' one. If ℂ is replaced by an arbitrary algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0, the same statement holds for the algebraic fundamental group, the one classifying étale coverings: the Lefschetz principle reduces us to assuming k = ℂ, in which case the algebraic fundamental group is the profinite completion of the genuine fundamental group. In arbitrary characteristic one has the variant:

THEOREM 2 (Fulton [3]).- Let k be an algebraically closed field and, over k, let C ⊂ ℙ² be a plane curve whose only singularities are double points with distinct tangents. Then the tame fundamental group of ℙ² - C is abelian.

In other words, coverings (in the sense of 0.2) of ℙ², ramified only along C and tamely ramified, are abelian. Recall that tameness of the ramification is tested after base change from ℙ² to its localizations at the generic points of the irreducible components of C. These localizations are traits (spectra of discrete valuation rings).

Suppose k has characteristic p > 0. If C is as in Theorem 2, there always exists in relative projective space ℙ² over Spec(W(k)) a relative normal-crossings divisor C̃ whose special fiber is C (see, for example, Mumford, Appendix to Ch. VIII of [9]). This makes it possible to deduce Theorem 2 from Theorem 1 by a specialization argument.

Once one knows that π₁(ℙ²(ℂ) - C) is abelian, homological arguments immediately give its structure: if C is the union of irreducible curves of degrees d₁, ..., dᵣ, then π₁(ℙ²(ℂ) - C) is the quotient of ℤʳ by the subgroup generated by the element (d₁, ..., dᵣ).

In his proof of Theorem 2, Fulton uses, on the one hand, methods introduced by Abhyankar [1] to prove the special case of Theorem 2 in which the irreducible components of C are assumed smooth - methods very clearly presented here by Serre ([7]) - and, on the other hand, Theorem 3 below. An analysis of the proof then enabled the expositor to give a variant yielding Theorem 1.

Abhyankar and Fulton both use instances of the principle that, in algebraic geometry, what is very mobile is connected. Let C ⊂ ℙ² be as in Theorem 2, let D be an irreducible component of C, and let f : X → ℙ² be a covering ramified only along C and tamely ramified. Since D ⊂ ℙ² is very mobile, f⁻¹(D) is connected. More precisely, the divisor D ⊂ ℙ² is ample, hence the divisor f⁻¹(D) ⊂ X is also ample because f is finite, and one applies Bertini. By a local study of f, Abhyankar shows that if D is smooth then (f⁻¹(D))red is smooth as well, and concludes that f⁻¹(D) is irreducible.

In the general case, let g : D̃ → D be the normalization of D. The same local study shows that the reduced fiber product (X ×_{ℙ²} D̃)red is smooth. It is therefore the normalization of f⁻¹(D). If it can be shown to be connected, it follows that f⁻¹(D) is irreducible, and one can repeat the end of Abhyankar's proof as presented in [7].

Recall the definition of the fiber product: if h : X × D̃ → ℙ² × ℙ² is the product of the maps f : X → ℙ² and g : D̃ → D ⊂ ℙ², then the fiber product X ×_{ℙ²} D̃ is the inverse image h⁻¹(Δ) of the diagonal. Since ℙ² has many automorphisms, the diagonal Δ ⊂ ℙ² × ℙ² is very mobile, and h⁻¹(Δ) is connected. This completes the proof. More precisely, one applies to h the special case r = 2, m = 2 of the following theorem:

THEOREM 3 (W. Fulton and J. Hansen [4]).- Let P = (ℙᵐ)ʳ be the product of r copies of projective space ℙᵐ, let δ be the diagonal map from ℙᵐ to P, let Δ = δ(ℙᵐ) be the diagonal, let Z be a complete irreducible variety, let h : Z → P, let n = dim h(Z), and let c = (r - 1)m be the codimension of Δ in P. If n - c ≥ 1, then h⁻¹(Δ) is connected.

This theorem has many other applications, for which I refer to [4] and to the article of T. Gaffney and R. Lazarsfeld [5].

At the end of this introduction, we explain by an example the method used to transpose Fulton's proof of Theorem 2 into a proof

of Theorem 1. The example is this: how to transpose Abhyankar's arguments to prove Theorem 1 in the special case where C is smooth (hence irreducible).

Let U be a tubular neighborhood of C in ℙ²(ℂ), let U* = U - C, and let u ∈ U*. For every covering f : X → ℙ²(ℂ) ramified only along C, one has

(f⁻¹(C) connected) ⇔ (f⁻¹(U) connected) ⇔ (f⁻¹(U*) connected).

The key result - that for every covering X the curve f⁻¹(C) is connected - is therefore equivalent to the following: for every finite quotient H of π₁(ℙ²(ℂ) - C,u), the composite map

π₁(U*,u) —j*→ π₁(ℙ²(ℂ) - C,u) → H

is surjective. A Morse-theoretic argument proves more: the map j* : π₁(U*,u) → π₁(ℙ²(ℂ) - C,u) is surjective.

After choosing a Riemannian metric on ℙ²(ℂ), for ε > 0 sufficiently small one may take U to be the image under the exponential map exp of the subbundle of balls of radius ε in the normal bundle of C in ℙ²(ℂ). For ε sufficiently small, exp identifies U* with an oriented punctured-disk bundle over C, giving an exact sequence

ℤ → π₁(U*,u) → π₁(C,ū) → 1

(ū is the image of u). The image of ℤ is central; the image of 1 ∈ ℤ is represented by a small loop γ going once around C in the positive direction.

Since j* is surjective, γ also defines a central element of π₁(ℙ²(ℂ) - C,u). The quotient of π₁(ℙ²(ℂ) - C,u) by the normal subgroup generated by γ (in this case, the cyclic subgroup generated by γ) is π₁(ℙ²(ℂ),u) = {e}, and the special case of the theorem under consideration follows.

0. Terminology

0.1. Connected means connected and nonempty. The same convention applies to irreducible.

0.2. A covering of a scheme S, assumed normal and connected, is a morphism f : T → S whose source T is normal and connected and whose restriction to a dense open subset of T is étale.

0.3. Throughout the rest of this exposition we work over ℂ. We shall write simply ℙⁿ for ℙⁿ(ℂ). All schemes considered are assumed separated.

1. Theorems of Lefschetz and Bertini type

The special case of 1.1 below in which Z ⊂ ℙⁿ is the complement of a hypersurface is proved by Hamm and Lê [6], using Morse theory. Our aim in this section is to deduce from it the variant 1.6 of Theorem 3.

Assertion 1.1.- Let Z ⊂ ℙⁿ be a nonempty Zariski-open subset. If H is a general hyperplane, the natural map πᵢ(Z ∩ H) → πᵢ(Z) is bijective for i < n - 1 and surjective for i = n - 1.

Assertion 1.1 is stated in [2], but Cheniot's proof covers only the case in which the complement of Z has codimension ≥ 2. Under this hypothesis, Z and Z ∩ H are simply connected, and it is harmless to work, as he does, with the Hᵢ rather than the πᵢ. The case i = 1 can also be deduced from [6] or [2 bis].

Recall that the adjective “general,” qualifying an element H of an irreducible algebraic variety S (here the dual projective space ℙⁿ∨), is a quantifier. It means that there exists a nonempty (hence dense) Zariski-open subset S' of S such that for every H in S', ....

1.2.- Let Y ⊂ ℙⁿ × ℙⁿ∨ be the space of pairs (z,H) such that z ∈ Z and z ∈ H. The isotopy theorem, applied to the second projection pr₂ : Y → ℙⁿ∨, gives a nonempty Zariski-open subset U of ℙⁿ∨ over which Y is a topologically locally trivial fiber space. It is enough to take U to be the set of hyperplanes transverse to the strata of an algebraic Whithney stratification of the complement of Z in ℙⁿ. Locally over U, after choosing a local trivialization of this fiber space, the inclusion Z ∩ H = pr₂⁻¹({H}) into Z appears as a continuously H-dependent map from a fixed space into Z. Thus the conclusion of 1.1 can hold for one H in U only if it holds for all of them, and 1.1 is equivalent to saying that it holds for every H in U.

Suppose that Z depends on parameters: take an irreducible scheme S and an open subset Z of S × ℙⁿ; set pr₂ pr₁⁻¹({s}) = Z(s), and assume every Z(s) is nonempty. Let Y ⊂ S × ℙⁿ × ℙⁿ∨ be the space of triples (s,z,H) such that z ∈ Z(s) and z ∈ H. The isotopy theorem, applied to the projection of Y onto S × ℙⁿ∨ (respectively, of Z onto S), gives a nonempty Zariski-open subset U of S × ℙⁿ∨ (respectively V of S) over which Y (respectively Z) is a topologically locally trivial fiber space.

As above, if s ∈ V and (s,H) ∈ U, the conclusion of 1.1 holds for Z(s) and H. This parameterized variant of 1.1 will be used implicitly in the proof of 1.4.

I conjecture more generally:

Conjecture 1.3.- Let Z be smooth and connected of dimension n, let f : Z → ℙᴺ be a morphism with finite fibers, let c be an integer, and let L be a linear subspace of ℙᴺ of

codimension c, with n* = n - c. Choose a Riemannian metric on ℙᴺ, and let V(ε) be the set of points p of ℙᴺ such that d(p,L) < ε. Then, for ε sufficiently small, the natural map

πᵢ(f⁻¹(V(ε))) → πᵢ(Z)

is bijective for i < n* and surjective for i = n*.

For general L, the inclusion of f⁻¹(L) into f⁻¹(V(ε)) is, for ε sufficiently small, a homotopy equivalence: 1.3 is indeed a generalization of 1.1.

If f is no longer assumed quasi-finite, and if the set of points of ℙᴺ where the fiber of f has dimension k has dimension φ(k), then n* should be redefined as

n* = 2 dim Z - sup(2k + φ(k) + inf(φ(k), c - 1)) - 1.

Conjecture 1.3 should moreover follow from a more precise statement saying that Z is obtained from f⁻¹(V(ε)) by attaching handles that kill spheres of dimension ≥ n*.

We shall be content with weaker results than 1.3. We deduce them from the special case of 1.1 in which Z is the complement of a hypersurface.

Lemma 1.4.- Let Z be normal and connected, let f : Z → ℙᴺ be a morphism, let n be the dimension of f(Z), and let c be an integer. Assume n - c ≥ 1. If L is a general linear subspace of ℙᴺ of codimension c, then f⁻¹(L) is connected and, for z ∈ f⁻¹(L), the natural map from π₁(f⁻¹(L),z) to π₁(Z,z) is surjective.

One may replace Z by a nonempty Zariski-open subset Z': for general L, f⁻¹(L) is still normal, and Z' (respectively Z' ∩ f⁻¹(L)) is obtained from Z (respectively f⁻¹(L)) by removing an algebraic subset with empty interior. By normality, this does not change π₀, can only enlarge π₁, and one considers the commutative diagram

π₁(Z' ∩ f⁻¹(L),z)  ↠  π₁(f⁻¹(L),z)
          ↓                         ↓
π₁(Z',z)              ↠  π₁(Z,z).

In particular, we may and do assume that Z is smooth. A reader interested only in the proof of Theorem 1 could in fact have assumed this from the outset; throughout the remainder of the section, that reader may replace “normal” by “smooth.”

After shrinking Z, we may and do assume that f(Z) is locally closed and that Z is a topologically locally trivial fiber space over f(Z).

If c = 1 and f is dominant, then f(Z) is a Zariski-open subset of ℙᴺ - after shrinking Z, we may assume it is the complement of a hypersurface - and it remains only to apply 1.1 to f(Z) and compare the long exact homotopy sequences for Z → f(Z) and f⁻¹(L) → L ∩ f(Z).

Continue to assume c = 1. If f is not dominant, let A be a

linear subspace of dimension N - n - 1, let B be the projective space of linear subspaces of dimension N - n containing A, and let q : ℙᴺ - A → B send x to the subspace containing it. For A disjoint from \overline{f(Z)}, the restriction of q to \overline{f(Z)} is a finite morphism, hence dominant because dim \overline{f(Z)} = dim B, and qf : Z → B is dominant. Applying the lemma to qf with c = 1 gives the conclusion of the lemma for a general hyperplane L among those containing A. Since A is only required to lie in a dense open subset of a suitable Grassmannian, the conclusion of the lemma also holds for general L (cf. 1.2).

The proof is completed by induction on c: a general linear subspace of codimension c - 1 in a general hyperplane is a general linear subspace of codimension c (cf. 1.2).

Lemma 1.5.- Let Z, f, n, and c be as in 1.4. Every linear subspace L of ℙᴺ of codimension c has a fundamental system of open neighborhoods V such that f⁻¹(V) is connected and, for z ∈ f⁻¹(V), the natural map from π₁(f⁻¹(V),z) to π₁(Z,z) is surjective.

Let Gr be the Grassmannian of linear subspaces of ℙᴺ of codimension c, let Y ⊂ Z × Gr be the set of pairs (z,L) such that f(z) ∈ L, and let G be a nonempty Zariski-open subset of Gr such that over G, Y is a topologically locally trivial fiber space. The conclusion of 1.4 then holds for L ∈ G (cf. 1.2).

For every open subset U of Gr, write U* for the open subset of ℙᴺ that is the union of the L ∈ U. We shall prove that if U is connected, the conclusion of 1.5 holds for V = U*. The lemma will follow.

Let us prove that if U is connected, f⁻¹(U*) is connected as well. The intersection U' = U ∩ G is connected, since it is obtained from U by removing a triangulable subset of real codimension ≥ 2. By 1.4, the union f⁻¹(U'*) of the f⁻¹(L) for L ∈ U' is therefore connected. We shall show that it is dense in f⁻¹(U*).

The image f(Z) of Z is not contained in the complement F of G*: since n - c ≥ 0, the L ∈ G meet f(Z). If z ∈ Z, the image of any neighborhood of z is not contained in F; otherwise the image of Z would be contained in F by analytic continuation. If z ∈ f⁻¹(U*), there are therefore points z' arbitrarily near z such that f(z') ∈ G*. In the set of L ∈ Gr containing z', the trace of G is dense, since it is nonempty. If z ∈ f⁻¹(L), with L ∈ U, this makes it possible to find z' as above lying in some f⁻¹(L'), with L' in G arbitrarily close to L. In particular one may take L' ∈ U', in which case z' ∈ f⁻¹(U'*). This proves the density of f⁻¹(U'*) in f⁻¹(U*) and the connectedness of f⁻¹(U*).

Finally let L ∈ U'. We have f⁻¹(L) ⊂ f⁻¹(U*) ⊂ Z. By 1.4, π₁(f⁻¹(L)) maps onto π₁(Z). A fortiori the same is true for π₁(f⁻¹(U*)).

We shall deduce from this a variant of Theorem 3.

Return to the proof of 1.6. Apply 1.5 to h : Z → B̄_α and to Δ̄_α. It follows that Δ̄_α has an arbitrarily small open neighborhood V_α such that h⁻¹(V_α) = h⁻¹(V_α ∩ B_α) is connected and its π₁ maps onto that of Z. By 1.7, whatever the neighborhood U of Δ in P, V_α can be chosen so that V_α ∩ B_α ⊂ U.

The union V of the open subsets V_α ∩ B_α of P is an arbitrarily small neighborhood of Δ. Hypothesis b) on the H_α ensures that the intersection of the V_α ∩ B_α meets h(Z). Hence h⁻¹(V), a union of connected open subsets h⁻¹(V_α) with nonempty common intersection, is connected. Since the π₁ of one of the h⁻¹(V_α) maps onto that of Z, a fortiori the same is true for h⁻¹(V), and this completes the proof.

2. Proof of Theorem 1

2.1.- Let C ⊂ ℙ² be a reduced plane curve, let D be an irreducible component of C, let C' = \overline{(C - D)} be the union of the other components, let Sing(C) be the set of singular points of C, and let D* = D - Sing(C). Choose a base point O ∈ ℙ² - C, and let γ be a loop in ℙ² - C of the following type: γ goes from O along a path ch to a point p' near a point p of D*, goes once around D* in the positive direction, and returns to O along ch⁻¹. Since D* is connected, all loops of this type are conjugate. The quotient of π₁(ℙ² - C,O) by the normal subgroup they generate is π₁(ℙ² - C').

PROPOSITION 2.2.- Suppose that the singular points of C lying on D are double points with distinct tangents. Then γ is central in π₁(ℙ² - C,O).

Let j be the inclusion of ℙ² - C into ℙ², let g : D̃ → D be the normalization of D, and apply 1.6 to

h = j × g : (ℙ² - C) × D̃ → ℙ² × ℙ².

To describe conveniently the inverse images of certain neighborhoods of the diagonal, choose on ℙ² a Riemannian structure such that, near each

If (u,v) ∈ (ℙ² - C) × D̃ lies in the inverse image of a sufficiently small neighborhood of the diagonal, that is, if u and v are sufficiently close, then u is near D and one can drop a short perpendicular from u to D. When u is near Sing(D), there are even two such perpendiculars, one for each branch. Choose the one whose foot ū is close to v on D̃:

The point ū lies in D*.

Conversely, let ε > 0 be sufficiently small, and let q : U* → D* be the punctured-disk subbundle of the normal bundle of D* in ℙ² consisting of nonzero normal vectors of length < ε. Let E be the set of pairs (x,v) with x ∈ U*, v ∈ D̃, and d(q(x),v) < ε (distance measured on D̃). The map pr₁ : E → U* is a homotopy equivalence and has the space of pairs (x,q(x)) as a section. The map exp : (x,v) ↦ (exp(x),v) from E to (ℙ² - C) × D̃ identifies E with the inverse image of a neighborhood of Δ, and as ε → 0 one obtains inverse images of a fundamental system of neighborhoods. Applying 1.6, one finds that for every O ∈ U*, exp and q induce a surjection

(exp,q)* : π₁(U*,O) ↠ π₁(ℙ² - C,exp(O)) × π₁(D̃,q(O)).

There is an exact homotopy sequence

ℤ → π₁(U*,O) → π₁(D*,q(O)) → 1.

The image of ℤ is central; the image of 1 ∈ ℤ is represented by a small loop going once around D* in the positive direction. Since (exp,q)*, and hence exp* : π₁(U*,O) → π₁(ℙ² - C,exp(O)), is surjective, this loop also defines a central element of π₁(ℙ² - C,exp(O)). It is γ.

2.3 Proof of Theorem 1: For every irreducible component D of C, let γ(D) be the corresponding central element of π₁(ℙ² - C,O). The quotient of π₁(ℙ² - C,O) by the - central - subgroup generated by the γ(D) is π₁(ℙ²,O) = {e}. The theorem follows.
